faq.q: What pushes water up a siphon?
faq.a: The air pressing on the water in the tank. Water falling down the outlet side lowers the pressure inside the tube, so the air pressure outside pushes water up the short side.
asks: How can water flow uphill in a tube?

faq.q: Why must the end of a siphon be lower?
faq.a: The outlet must be below the water surface in the tank so the falling side is longer and heavier. If it were higher, the water would flow backwards instead.
asks: What happens if the bucket is higher than the tank?

faq.q: Why must the siphon tube be full of water?
faq.a: A siphon needs an unbroken column of water. An air bubble at the top breaks the column, and the flow stops.
asks: Why do you have to suck a siphon to start it?

faq.q: How high can a siphon lift water?
faq.a: Air pressure can only push water up about 10 metres, so a water siphon cannot climb over a hump taller than that. In practice the limit is a little lower.
asks: Is there a limit to a siphon?

faq.a: People use them to empty fish tanks, drain ponds and move fuel, and most toilets use a siphon to empty the bowl.
asks: What is a siphon used for?

facts: A siphon only works if its outlet is lower than the surface of the water it is drawing from.
At sea level, air pressure limits a water siphon to rising about 10 metres above the water surface.

quiz.say: A siphon is set up, but the end of the tube is lifted above the water in the tank. What happens?
quiz.show: A siphon is set up, but the end of the tube is lifted above the water in the tank. What happens?
quiz.why: The outlet must be below the tank surface. Lift it higher and the falling side is no longer heavier, so the flow stops or goes back.

wrong.1: Raising the outlet slows and stops the flow; it does not speed it up.
wrong.2: There is no extra pressure to spray water upwards.
